title: Where the team leader role starts and stops
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: New and experienced team leaders and crew leads who direct a small group of workers on cleaning jobs.
learningOutcomes: Name the main duties a crew leader carries on a cleaning team.
Explain how a team leader's role differs from a manager's role in general terms.
Separate core, secondary and other-person tasks in a written role description.

instruction.heading: What the role is for
instruction.body: A team leader keeps a small group moving toward one shared result, such as finishing a set of rooms to standard before a handover time. The leader handles the practical problems that slow the work and the interpersonal problems that come between people. On a cleaning crew this means knowing who is doing which part of the job, building the day's plan, checking progress as the shift runs, and telling the supervisor where the job stands. The leader also gives people feedback so they can improve.

instruction.heading: How it differs from a manager's role
instruction.body: Both roles settle problems, allocate tasks and track progress. The distinction lies in scale and authority. A team leader usually works with a smaller group, while a manager may oversee several groups and the leaders within them. Decisions about discipline, formal performance outcomes and pay are commonly held above the team leader, but the exact split depends on how the business is set up and how each worker is engaged.

instruction.heading: Keeping core work separate from everything else
instruction.body: Every role collects extra requests. Some are reasonable and some belong to someone else. Write down the tasks that the role must deliver, the tasks that support them, and the tasks that sit with another person or team. Extra work is sometimes needed for a short time, but the lead is judged mainly on the core tasks. Practise declining a request in a calm, specific way, explain the reason, and offer to take the question to the supervisor when the answer is not yours to give.

procedure: Write the core tasks of the role on a single page, using plain verbs such as plan, brief, check and report.
List the secondary tasks that support the core tasks, such as keeping the equipment trolley stocked.
List any tasks that belong to the office, a supervisor or another team and mark them as not yours.
Walk through the list with your supervisor and mark which decisions you may make alone and which need approval.
Share the agreed list with your crew so that everyone knows who to ask for what.
Review the list when the mix of jobs changes, or when a new service is added.

workedExamples.situation: A crew lead on a bond clean is asked by the office to quote new jobs, chase unpaid invoices and also lead the crew on site.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which tasks stay with the crew lead, which return to the office, and how should the lead first reply?
workedExamples.reasoning: Leading the crew on site and reporting progress is core. Quoting and invoice follow-up belong to the office unless the supervisor formally moves them. The reply should name the on-site duties, ask the supervisor to confirm any change in writing, and avoid silently taking on the extra work.

equipmentAndPpe: No specialist equipment. Use the site's standard PPE and the crew's agreed checklist or notebook.

commonErrors.error: Accepting every request so the lead looks helpful, which leaves the core work late.
commonErrors.prevention: Check each new request against the written role list before agreeing to it.

commonErrors.error: Assuming that leading a crew includes decisions about pay or discipline.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the decision boundary with the supervisor and record the answer.

commonErrors.error: Declining a request with no reason, which damages trust.
commonErrors.prevention: Give one specific reason and an offer to refer the question onward.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A lead's authority to stop work on site comes from the business's own procedure. Confirm it before the first shift.

qualityStandard: The learner produces a role description with three separate lists: core tasks, secondary tasks and tasks belonging to others.
The learner names at least two decisions that need supervisor approval, using the business's own terms.
documentationEvidence: Signed role description with the supervisor's review date.
Record of any request declined or referred, with the reason given.
summary: A team leader coordinates a small group toward a shared result and reports progress upward.
Discipline, formal performance outcomes and pay usually sit above the team leader, subject to the business's setup.
Write the role down, separate core from other work, and review it when the job mix changes.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which task most clearly falls within a crew leader's main duties on a cleaning team?
options: Setting the day's plan for the crew and tracking progress on each job
Deciding a worker's pay rise without consulting anyone today
Approving new supplier contracts for the whole business today
Hiring and dismissing workers across all sites and setting all the pay rates

knowledgeChecks.question: How does a team leader usually differ from a manager?
options: A team leader makes the final pay decision for the crew each month and sets the rates
A team leader usually works with a smaller group, while a manager may oversee several groups
A manager assigns work to the crew only through the team leader and never speaks to the crew
Insurance cover for the whole business falls to the team leader and the accounts

knowledgeChecks.question: A supervisor asks a crew lead to take on quoting as well as leading jobs. What is the best first response?
options: Accept all the extra work to look helpful and skip the crew checks for the day
Refuse without giving any reason and tell the crew to do the quoting
Check the role list and agree with the supervisor which tasks stay with the lead
Quietly stop the crew work so the quoting can be done and not tell the crew why
